documentation.content:
# Concrete Compressive Strength

This dataset explores how concrete mixture composition and curing age relate to compressive strength and provides a governed continuous-regression model for predicting strength on the original MPa scale.

The objective is not only to obtain a numerical prediction, but also to document the analytical path from understanding the dataset to evaluating a continuous-regression model on previously unseen data.

## Dataset overview

Each row represents a concrete mixture and curing-age observation described by eight numerical predictive features.

| Item | Value |
| --- | ---: |
| Concrete observations | 1,030 |
| Source columns | 9 |
| Predictive features | 8 |
| Target | `Concrete compressive strength` |
| Target unit | MPa |
| Problem type | Continuous regression |
| Source | UCI Machine Learning Repository |
| UCI dataset ID | `165` |

The eight predictive features are:

| Feature | Unit |
| --- | --- |
| Cement | kg/m³ |
| Blast Furnace Slag | kg/m³ |
| Fly Ash | kg/m³ |
| Water | kg/m³ |
| Superplasticizer | kg/m³ |
| Coarse Aggregate | kg/m³ |
| Fine Aggregate | kg/m³ |
| Age | days |

The target is never exposed as a predictive feature.

The seven mixture-composition variables describe the quantities of binder materials, water, admixture, and aggregates, while `Age` describes the curing time associated with the measured sample.

## Analytical question

The analysis investigates two related questions:

1. **How are concrete mixture composition and curing age associated with observed compressive strength?**
2. **How effectively can those measurements be used to predict compressive strength for previously unseen observations?**

The response is a quantitative continuous measurement expressed in MPa.

Exploratory relationships between individual inputs and compressive strength should be interpreted as predictive associations within this dataset rather than as evidence that changing one component in isolation will causally produce a particular strength.

Concrete performance depends on interacting material, proportion, curing, testing, and environmental conditions that are not fully represented by a simple univariate relationship.

## Data quality and preparation

The source contains 1,030 observations, eight numerical predictors, and one continuous target.

All 1,030 observations have a present and finite target value.

The preparation policy preserves the released source observations without generic row removal, imputation, clipping, winsorization, target binning, or automatic outlier deletion.

A source-metadata inconsistency is explicitly handled for `Blast Furnace Slag`: UCI metadata labels the variable as integer, while the materialized source contains valid decimal measurements. The released decimal values are therefore preserved rather than rounded or truncated.

The exploration also identifies exact row-equality groups and repeated feature profiles. Because the source provides no observation identifier, equality is not treated as proof that two rows represent the same physical concrete specimen. These observations are preserved and carried forward as evidence rather than automatically deduplicated.

The governed split uses random seed `42` and a shuffled, non-stratified continuous-regression partition:

| Partition | Rows | Approximate share | Purpose |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Train | 721 | 70% | Model fitting |
| Validation | 154 | 15% | Governed model evaluation |
| Test | 155 | 15% | Final holdout evaluation |

The test partition remains outside model selection and is accessed only for final evaluation after the model configuration has been frozen.

## Target distribution

Observed concrete compressive strength ranges from **2.33 MPa** to **82.60 MPa**.

| Statistic | Value |
| --- | ---: |
| Minimum | 2.33 MPa |
| Mean | 35.8180 MPa |
| Median | 34.4450 MPa |
| Maximum | 82.60 MPa |
| Standard deviation | 16.7057 MPa |
| Interquartile range | 22.4250 MPa |

Four observations fall above the exploratory upper 1.5-IQR fence.

These values are treated as descriptive extreme-value signals rather than automatic outlier-removal candidates.

![Concrete compressive strength target distribution](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FabioAguiar/dataset-study-concrete-compressives-strength/main/docs/images/target_distribution.png)

Preserving the original continuous target scale keeps model error directly interpretable in MPa.

## Key exploratory findings

### Curing age shows the strongest monotonic association with strength

`Age` has the strongest observed monotonic feature-to-target association in the exploratory analysis.

Its Spearman correlation with compressive strength is approximately **0.5960**, while its Pearson correlation is approximately **0.3289**.

The difference between the two measures is consistent with a relationship that is informative but not adequately summarized as a purely linear trend.

`Cement` shows the strongest Pearson correlation with the target at approximately **0.4978**.

`Superplasticizer` also shows a positive exploratory association, while `Water` shows a negative association.

| Feature | Pearson | Spearman | Maximum absolute association |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Age | 0.3289 | 0.5960 | **0.5960** |
| Cement | 0.4978 | 0.4776 | **0.4978** |
| Superplasticizer | 0.3661 | 0.3478 | **0.3661** |
| Water | -0.2896 | -0.3084 | **0.3084** |

![Univariate feature-to-target associations](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FabioAguiar/dataset-study-concrete-compressives-strength/main/docs/images/feature_target_association_ranking.png)

These are univariate descriptive relationships. They do not establish causality, prescribe mixture changes, or determine which variables should be retained by a predictive model.

### No feature pair reaches the predefined redundancy threshold

The eight numerical predictors contain relationships expected from concrete mixture composition, but none of the 28 feature pairs reaches the study's predefined strong-association threshold of `0.80`.

No pair reaches the stricter Pearson redundancy-review threshold of `0.90`.

![Numerical feature correlation heatmap](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FabioAguiar/dataset-study-concrete-compressives-strength/main/docs/images/numerical_feature_correlation_heatmap.png)

The complete validated feature set is therefore retained for model comparison.

The absence of a threshold-level pair does not imply that the inputs are statistically independent; it only means that the predefined exploratory redundancy criterion was not triggered.

### The regression structure contains meaningful nonlinear signals

The exploratory regression diagnostics identify three features for which adding a quadratic term produces a notable in-sample adjusted-R² gain:

* `Age`;
* `Water`;
* `Blast Furnace Slag`.

`Age` produces the largest quadratic adjusted-R² gain, approximately `0.1480`.

![Regression nonlinearity signals](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FabioAguiar/dataset-study-concrete-compressives-strength/main/docs/images/regression_nonlinearity_signals.png)

The analysis also identifies four feature pairs meeting the predefined exploratory interaction-review threshold:

* `Blast Furnace Slag` × `Superplasticizer`;
* `Fly Ash` × `Coarse Aggregate`;
* `Cement` × `Blast Furnace Slag`;
* `Blast Furnace Slag` × `Water`.

![Pairwise regression interaction signals](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FabioAguiar/dataset-study-concrete-compressives-strength/main/docs/images/regression_interaction_signals.png)

These adjusted-R² gains are in-sample structural diagnostics only.

They do not estimate future predictive performance, prove physical interaction mechanisms, or prescribe polynomial or engineered features. Their role is to motivate leakage-safe comparison between simple additive models and more flexible regression families.

## Model selection evidence

The companion Concrete study compares a prior-only regression baseline with four machine-learning model families:

* Ridge;
* Decision Tree;
* Random Forest;
* HistGradientBoosting.

Model selection uses validation MAE as the primary metric, with RMSE, R², and median absolute error as supporting evidence.

| Model | Validation MAE ↓ | Validation RMSE ↓ | Validation R² | Validation MedAE ↓ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Dummy median | 12.8145 | 15.8699 | -0.0005 | 11.2600 |
| Ridge | 8.5944 | 10.7533 | 0.5406 | 7.1671 |
| Decision Tree | 4.2860 | 6.5247 | 0.8309 | 2.9000 |
| Random Forest | 3.7689 | 5.4146 | 0.8835 | 2.5385 |
| **HistGradientBoosting** | **2.7417** | **4.0870** | **0.9336** | **1.8033** |

`HistGradientBoostingRegressor` produces the lowest validation MAE and is selected under the predefined deterministic selection policy.

No practical tie is detected under the study's `0.10 MPa` MAE tolerance.

The selected configuration retains all eight features and uses:

```text
model family         = hist_gradient_boosting
l2_regularization    = 1.0
learning_rate        = 0.1
max_iter             = 300
max_leaf_nodes       = 15
min_samples_leaf     = 10
random_seed          = 42
```

This evidence supports the use of a flexible nonlinear model and is consistent with the nonlinear structure observed during exploration.

The governed Atlas execution contract freezes the same model family and configuration rather than performing AutoML or unrestricted search during the active Atlas training run.

## Active Atlas release evaluation

The active Atlas release is:

`release-20260820-001`

The release evaluates the governed model once on the previously sealed final test partition containing **155 observations**.

| Metric | Final test |
| --- | ---: |
| **MAE ↓** | **2.0453 MPa** |
| RMSE ↓ | **2.9740 MPa** |
| R² | **0.9694** |

The final test partition is recorded as unused for fitting, model selection, hyperparameter selection, or decision-rule adjustment.

These are the authoritative performance metrics for the active Atlas release.

The companion study provides the scientific model-selection rationale and reproducible analytical evidence, while the Atlas-native release provides the metrics associated with the model currently exposed by Atlas.

The results describe performance under the current governed random-snapshot evaluation. They do not establish performance under temporal shift, different concrete populations, different laboratory procedures, or production deployment.

## Understanding the highlighted metrics

### MAE — 2.0453 MPa

Mean Absolute Error measures the average absolute distance between the predicted and observed compressive-strength values.

An MAE of `2.0453 MPa` means that, across the final holdout observations, the model's predictions differ from the measured values by about 2.05 MPa on average when error direction is ignored.

Because MAE remains on the original target scale, it is directly interpretable in MPa.

**Lower values are better.**

MAE is the primary governed evaluation metric for the active Concrete execution contract and is therefore the highlighted regression score in Atlas.

### RMSE — 2.9740 MPa

Root Mean Squared Error also measures prediction error on the original MPa scale, but it gives greater weight to larger errors because residuals are squared before aggregation.

It is therefore useful alongside MAE for identifying whether a smaller number of larger misses materially affect overall error.

**Lower values are better.**

RMSE should not be compared directly with MAE as though the numerically smaller metric were automatically superior; the two metrics summarize error differently.

### R² — 0.9694

R² compares the model's squared prediction error with a baseline that predicts the target mean.

A final-test value of approximately `0.9694` indicates that the model accounts for a large share of the target variation in this particular holdout partition.

**Higher values are generally better.**

R² is dimensionless and should be interpreted together with error metrics on the original MPa scale.

A high R² does not imply causal understanding, guaranteed engineering accuracy, or equivalent performance on future populations.

## Continuous-regression inference experience

The Atlas inference form receives eight numerical inputs covering concrete mixture composition and curing age.

The presentation organizes the inputs into four groups:

* **Binder Materials** — Cement, Blast Furnace Slag, and Fly Ash;
* **Water & Admixture** — Water and Superplasticizer;
* **Aggregates** — Coarse Aggregate and Fine Aggregate;
* **Curing** — Age.

The governed model returns a single continuous numerical prediction:

`Predicted compressive strength`

The result is presented on the original **MPa** scale.

Unlike classification problems, continuous regression has:

* no target classes;
* no positive class;
* no class-probability distribution;
* no classification threshold;
* no `argmax` decision rule.

The inference result is a point estimate produced by the trained model from the supplied numerical inputs.

Atlas does not currently present this estimate as a laboratory measurement, engineering certification, or uncertainty interval.

## What this dataset demonstrates

Concrete Compressive Strength extends the Atlas educational workflow into native continuous regression.

The project demonstrates:

* continuous numerical target contracts;
* preservation of the original target scale and unit;
* dataset understanding and exploratory regression analysis;
* evidence-backed data-quality decisions;
* deterministic train, validation, and test partitions;
* leakage protection and sealed final-test evaluation;
* comparison between linear, tree-based, ensemble, and boosting regressors;
* MAE-driven model selection;
* fixed-model governance rather than unrestricted AutoML;
* final holdout evaluation with regression-specific metrics;
* continuous numerical inference;
* contract-driven presentation of a regression result in MPa.

It therefore validates that Atlas predictive abstractions can represent numerical outcomes without importing binary or multiclass classification semantics.

## Limitations

Several important boundaries remain:

* the dataset contains only 1,030 observations;
* evaluation is based on a shuffled random snapshot rather than temporal, site-based, batch-based, or external validation;
* exploratory correlations and structural diagnostics do not establish causal material effects;
* the dataset does not capture every physical, environmental, production, curing, and testing factor that can influence concrete strength;
* repeated feature profiles and exact row matches are preserved because source identity cannot be established;
* the model produces a point prediction rather than a calibrated prediction interval;
* performance within the observed dataset does not establish safe extrapolation beyond the governed input domains;
* no production monitoring, drift policy, or scheduled retraining policy is established by this study;
* operational validity remains outside the educational scope;
* model predictions are not a substitute for laboratory testing, engineering review, material standards, or structural-safety procedures.

## Responsible interpretation

The evidence supports the following conclusion:

> In this dataset, concrete mixture composition and curing age contain strong predictive information for compressive strength. Exploratory diagnostics show meaningful nonlinear structure, and HistGradientBoosting provides the strongest validation performance among the compared model families. The active Atlas release uses a governed continuous-regression configuration with all eight predictive features and achieves a final-test MAE of approximately 2.0453 MPa, RMSE of approximately 2.9740 MPa, and R² of approximately 0.9694.

The Atlas inference experience should therefore be interpreted as an interactive demonstration of a governed continuous-regression workflow.

Its prediction is an educational model estimate on the MPa scale, not a certified material property or a replacement for physical testing and engineering judgment.
